edges.effect_quant: Across modern and older cohorts, prenatal valproate exposure consistently carries one of the strongest neurodevelopmental harm signals among antiseizure drugs. In a blinded 210-child cohort, developmental delay occurred in 39.6% of valproate-exposed children and valproate exposure was associated with OR 26.1 (95% CI 4.9-139) for developmental delay versus controls.
edges.population: children exposed to valproate in utero, usually for maternal epilepsy treatment
edges.mechanism: Valproate crosses the placenta and is linked to disrupted neuronal proliferation, folate-related pathways, and fetal brain development, producing higher risks of cognitive, language, behavioral, and neurodevelopmental disorders than many alternative antiseizure drugs.
edges.summary: The evidence that valproate in pregnancy harms offspring neurodevelopment is strong and consistent. Large contemporary registry data, blinded developmental cohorts, and comparative antiseizure-drug studies all place valproate at the high-risk end of the spectrum for autism, intellectual disability, ADHD, and broader developmental delay.
edges.caveats: Risk is not identical across dose levels or epilepsy populations, and some older studies had relatively small exposed samples. Even so, the direction of effect is unusually consistent compared with the more ambiguous data for several newer antiseizure drugs.
